headline: Zelenskyy urges support for paused Russia sanctions

sources.title: Zelenskyy urges backing for Russia sanctions put on hold by Trump (AP News)
Trump Waives Graham Act Sanctions On Russia Before They Take Effect (RFE/RL)
Trump signs order waiving Graham Act sanctions on Russia, drawing backlash from some lawmakers and Zelenskyy (ABC News)

chunks.text: On October 16, 2026, President Donald Trump signed an [[executive order]] about a new [[sanctions]] law against Russia. In it, he decided to {{hold off}} on almost all of the law's [[measures]]. They were due to start two days later. On October 17, Ukrainian President Zelenskyy called the decision [[unfortunate]]. He asked the law's supporters to {{speak up for}} it. He said the law could still help a lot.

verbs.wrong: To reject a law in a vote
verbs.why: Many families hold off on dinner until everyone arrives. Some companies hold off on hiring when sales are slow. Trump decided to hold off on almost all of the sanctions law's measures.

verbs.correct: To say openly that you support something
verbs.wrong: To ask a leader hard questions on TV
verbs.why: Parents often speak up for a new school lunch plan at meetings. A brave worker speaks up for a coworker who is treated unfairly. Zelenskyy asked the law's supporters to speak up for it.

chunks.text: Ukraine wants Washington to {{follow through}} on the law. Congress passed it by [[wide margins]], and Trump signed it in September. The law would {{go after}} Russian officials, banks and a [[shadow fleet]] of oil tankers. It also allows [[tariffs]] of up to 100 percent on the biggest buyers of Russian oil and gas. The law was written to help the United States {{stand up to}} Russia over the war.

verbs.correct: To do what you promised or planned to do
verbs.wrong: To read every page of a new law
verbs.why: A good leader always follows through on promises. Some cities never follow through on plans for new parks. Ukraine wants Washington to follow through on the sanctions law.

verbs.correct: To try to punish or stop someone
verbs.wrong: To check a list of names closely
verbs.why: Police go after drivers who use their phones. New tax rules go after companies that cheat. The law would go after Russian officials, banks and a shadow fleet of oil tankers.

verbs.correct: To firmly resist someone more powerful
verbs.wrong: To send soldiers to another country
verbs.why: A brave student stands up to a bully in class. Small nations sometimes stand up to their larger neighbors. The law was written to help the United States stand up to Russia over the war.

chunks.text: Trump told Congress that the pause was in the [[national interest]]. A White House [[spokesperson]] said that using the sanctions now would {{hold up}} [[peace talks]]. [[Lawmakers]] from both parties {{pushed back}}. A Democratic senator who helped write the law said the pause had nothing to do with national security. A Republican senator called it [[irresponsible]]. One Republican congressman welcomed the decision. A week earlier, Trump agreed to buy Russian [[diesel]] to try to lower [[fuel prices]].

verbs.correct: To make something slower or later
verbs.wrong: To move talks to another country
verbs.why: Heavy snow often holds up trains for hours. A missing signature holds up the sale of a house. A White House spokesperson said that using the sanctions now would hold up peace talks.
Teachers push back when a school cuts art classes. Many workers push back against strict new office rules. Lawmakers from both parties pushed back after Trump paused the sanctions.

chunks.text: Zelenskyy said that easing [[pressure]] only encourages Russia to {{keep up}} its attacks. On the night before his statement, Russia targeted more than 15 [[energy sites]] across Ukraine, he said. Each side said it {{shot down}} hundreds of the other's drones. The Associated Press says Russia attacks Ukraine's [[power grid]] each winter to {{wear down}} the country's [[will to fight]]. Zelenskyy also said the United States was working to {{set up}} a meeting with him, Trump and Putin.

verbs.why: Some neighbors keep up loud parties until midnight. In spring, the rain often keeps up all afternoon. Zelenskyy said that easing pressure only encourages Russia to keep up its attacks.
Air defense systems shoot down drones before they reach the city. Soldiers sometimes shoot down enemy helicopters near the border. Each side said it shot down hundreds of the other's drones.

verbs.wrong: To make someone angry very quickly
verbs.why: Long trips wear small children down. Months of hard work wear many nurses down. The Associated Press says Russia attacks Ukraine's power grid each winter to wear down the country's will to fight.

verbs.correct: To plan and arrange a meeting
verbs.wrong: To film a meeting for the news
verbs.why: An assistant sets up meetings for the manager every week. My office sets up a video call with new clients each Monday. Zelenskyy said the United States was working to set up a meeting with him, Trump and Putin.

ex: We held off on buying a car until prices fell.
The doctor told me to hold off on running for a week.
Let's hold off on painting the kitchen until spring.

vocab.def: To say openly that you support something
ex: Nobody spoke up for the plan at the meeting.
She always speaks up for better pay for nurses.
Will you speak up for my idea when the boss asks?

vocab.def: To do what you promised or planned to do
ex: If you make a promise to a child, follow through.
She said she would quit sugar, and she followed through.
The team never followed through on its plan to train more.

vocab.def: To try to punish or stop someone
ex: The bank went after people who never paid their loans.
The city plans to go after landlords who ignore safety rules.
Tax officials went after the company for unpaid taxes.

vocab.def: To firmly resist someone more powerful
ex: The workers stood up to the company and asked for fair pay.
It is hard for a small nation to stand up to a large army.
The town stood up to the big company and won in court.

vocab.def: To make something slower or later
ex: An accident held up traffic on the highway.
Bad weather held up the building work for a month.
Sorry I'm late. The meeting held me up.
Students pushed back when the college raised fees.
Parents pushed back hard against the new bus schedule.
Some doctors pushed back on the hospital's new policy.
The fans kept up their singing for the whole game.
If you keep up this pace, you'll finish early.
The workers kept up their strike for three weeks.
The navy shot down a missile over the sea.
The pilot was shot down during the war.
Air defense systems can shoot down most small drones.
The night shifts slowly wore him down.
Constant noise can wear you down.
The long strike wore down both the workers and the owners.

vocab.def: To plan and arrange a meeting
ex: I set up a meeting with my child's teacher.
Could you set up a video call for ten o'clock?
The two companies set up talks for next month.

wordDefs.def: An official rule a president makes without a vote in Congress
ex: The governor signed an executive order on school safety.
An executive order can be changed by the next president.
Lawyers are studying the new executive order on travel.

wordDefs.def: Official actions that limit trade or money to punish a country
ex: The sanctions made it hard for the country to sell its oil.
Some leaders want to end the sanctions.
Banks must follow the new sanctions.

wordDefs.def: Official actions taken to deal with a problem
ex: The city took new measures to cut crime.
Safety measures at the airport are very strict.
The school announced measures to save money.
It was an unfortunate mistake.
The game ended in an unfortunate way for our team.
It is unfortunate that the store closed.

wordDefs.def: Large differences in the number of votes
ex: The mayor won both elections by wide margins.
The plan passed by wide margins in the city council.
Polls show the senator leading by wide margins.

wordDefs.def: A group of ships that secretly carry goods to avoid rules
ex: Reporters followed one ship from the shadow fleet for weeks.
The shadow fleet often uses old tankers.
Officials want to stop the shadow fleet from reaching their ports.

wordDefs.def: Taxes on goods that come from other countries
ex: New tariffs made imported cars more expensive.
Farmers worry about tariffs on their exports.
The two countries agreed to cut tariffs.

wordDefs.def: What is good for a whole country
ex: The president said the new port was in the national interest.
Leaders often disagree about the national interest.
Protecting clean water is in the national interest.

wordDefs.def: A person who speaks officially for a group or company
ex: A spokesperson for the airline said the flight was safe.
The hospital's spokesperson answered questions from reporters.
A police spokesperson gave an update on the case.

wordDefs.def: Meetings where two sides try to end a war
ex: The peace talks lasted for three days.
Both leaders agreed to join peace talks.
Many people hope the peace talks will succeed.

wordDefs.def: People who are elected to make laws
ex: Lawmakers voted on the new budget last night.
Lawmakers in some states want to raise the minimum wage.
Lawmakers from both parties met with the governor.

wordDefs.def: Not thinking carefully about the results of your actions
ex: It is irresponsible to drive so fast in the rain.
The coach called the player's behavior irresponsible.
Leaving a small child alone is irresponsible.

wordDefs.def: A heavy fuel used by trucks, trains and some cars
ex: Most big trucks run on diesel.
The price of diesel went higher in the winter.
Our old car uses diesel, not gas.

wordDefs.def: How much people pay for gas and diesel
ex: High fuel prices make flights more expensive.
Fuel prices often change before a long weekend.
Farmers worry about rising fuel prices.

wordDefs.def: Strong influence used to make someone do something
ex: Pressure from parents made the school hire more teachers.
The workers used pressure to get better pay.
There is pressure on the city to fix the roads.

wordDefs.def: Places that make or carry power, such as power plants
ex: Guards protect the country's energy sites.
Storms damaged several energy sites on the coast.
New energy sites will use wind and sun.

wordDefs.def: The system of lines that carries electricity to homes
ex: A heat wave put stress on the power grid.
The storm damaged part of the power grid.
Engineers are working to make the power grid stronger.

wordDefs.def: The strong wish to keep fighting
ex: The team lost the game but kept its will to fight.
Long wars can weaken a nation's will to fight.
The boxer's will to fight surprised everyone.

mainIdea.s: Trump paused nearly all of a new law meant to punish Russia over its war in Ukraine. Zelenskyy called that unfortunate and asked its supporters to defend it while Russian attacks continue.
mainIdea.why: Trump decided to hold off on almost all of the law's measures. Zelenskyy asked supporters to speak up for it, saying easing pressure lets Russia keep up attacks.

mainIdea.s: Zelenskyy openly attacked Trump after the U.S. leader canceled a sanctions law on Russia. Congress is now quickly voting again to force the White House to use every penalty against Moscow.
mainIdea.why: Close, but Zelenskyy only called the pause unfortunate and asked supporters to speak up for the law. Lawmakers pushed back, but no new vote is described.

mainIdea.s: Ukraine and Russia signed a short deal to stop strikes on power plants before winter. Leaders from Europe and the United States helped arrange it at a summit held in a neutral country.
mainIdea.why: There is no deal. Russia targeted more than 15 energy sites, and the United States is only trying to set up a meeting with the three leaders.

tf.s: Trump decided to hold off on almost all of the new sanctions.
tf.why: He signed an executive order that paused nearly all of the law's measures two days before they were due to start.

tf.s: Zelenskyy asked the law's supporters to speak up for it.
tf.why: He called Trump's decision unfortunate and said the law could still help a lot.

tf.s: The law would go after Russian officials, banks and oil tankers.
tf.why: It targets officials, banks and a shadow fleet of tankers, and it allows tariffs on big buyers of Russian oil and gas.

tf.s: Lawmakers from both parties praised Trump's decision to pause the sanctions.
tf.why: Lawmakers from both parties pushed back. A Republican senator called the pause irresponsible.

tf.s: The White House said the sanctions would help the peace talks move faster.
tf.why: A spokesperson said that using the sanctions now would hold up peace talks, not make them faster.

tf.s: Zelenskyy said that easing pressure will make Russia stop its attacks.
tf.why: He said the opposite. Easing pressure only encourages Russia to keep up its attacks.

lines.text: Did you see that Trump paused those new sanctions on Russia?
I did. I was [[caught off guard]]. Didn't he sign that law himself?
He did, in September. Now he's decided to {{hold off}} on almost all of it.
Lawmakers from both parties {{pushed back}}. One Republican senator called it irresponsible.
Zelenskyy was careful. He called it unfortunate and asked people to {{speak up for}} the law.
What would the law actually do?
It would {{go after}} Russian officials, banks and those shadow fleet tankers.
The White House says using them now would {{hold up}} peace talks.
I guess both sides [[have a point]].
Maybe. But Zelenskyy says easing pressure lets Russia {{keep up}} its attacks.
The power grid attacks before winter must {{wear down}} people there, [[to put it mildly]].
Yes. Ukraine just wants Washington to {{follow through}}.
Is anything else happening [[in the meantime]]?
The U.S. is trying to {{set up}} a meeting with Zelenskyy, Trump and Putin.

expressions.def: Surprised by something because you were not ready for it
ex: I was caught off guard by the question.
Many drivers were caught off guard by the snow.

expressions.def: Messages or actions that seem to say two different things
ex: My boss keeps giving me mixed signals about the raise.

expressions.def: Used to say that someone's idea is partly right or fair
ex: You have a point. The bus is cheaper than the train.
I don't agree with him, but he has a point.

expressions.def: Used to say that the real situation is even stronger or worse
ex: The food was not great, to put it mildly.

expressions.def: Used to talk about the time while you wait for something else
ex: The doctor will see you soon. In the meantime, please sit down.
